messages.subject: Large data sets
parts:
Hi Phil,

Thanks as always for your continued work on this excellent package. I have a question for you about large data sets: I'm fitting some models to data sets of about 350,000 students. This takes quite a long time for each model, but there are no problems. I noticed that there's a large = TRUE option in the mirt function, so I tested it out the way it was suggested to be used in the manual:

> start.time <- proc.time()
> internaldat <- mirt(data = dat, model = 1, itemtype = "Rasch", large = TRUE)
> mod <- mirt(data = dat, model = 1, itemtype = "Rasch", large = internaldat)
> proc.time() - start.time
   user  system elapsed 
  78.66    1.60   80.58 

But I actually get slightly faster proc time if I don't use the large = TRUE step, presumably because then I'm only running the one call to mirt:

> start.time <- proc.time()
> mod <- mirt(data = dat, model = 1, itemtype = "Rasch")
> proc.time() - start.time
   user  system elapsed 
  76.50    1.45   78.14

If this feature doesn't cut down on fit time for a data set this large, that makes me think I'm misunderstanding its purpose. Can you please give some more information on what this option in intended to do and how to best make use of it?

And while we're on the topic, other than changing the TOL and quadpts options, do you have any other advice for speeding up proc times?

Thanks,
Jon

messages.author: b330c2028fed415b
messages.subject: Re: Large data sets
parts: The large option has to do with minimization how long it takes to obtain the unique vectors of response patterns and their associated frequencies. This is a function of a few things, such as the sample size, number of response options, but more importantly the length of the test. For long tests there is a good chance that many of the responses observed are already unique, so this reduced table may end up having close to the same number of rows as the initial observation data (hence, it's really just time consuming to compute it). Larger sample sizes, even in the millions, may not be problematic if the number of unique responses is small due to using a shorter test with fewer response options.
And while we're on the topic, other than changing the TOL and quadpts options, do you have any other advice for speeding up proc times?

Use Linux? I've noticed the estimation times are quite a bit smaller on Ubuntu than Windows 10 running the same hardware for some reason (maybe because everything must be complied on Linux and is therefore more efficient with the hardware, or it's just the OS itself that's better at computing). HTH.
 

Thanks,
Jon
